title: What long term tradeoffs are you encountering?
author: YesBoxStudios
selftext:
I am a game developer not using AI, but I am interested in how the industry is changing. I've been developing my game for almost 5 years. I started with SFML and an empty .cpp file (C++). 

I'm making a complex game, so one of the reasons I built my own engine is because I thought over the long term, the decision would benefit me. Organizing logic and data my way means I am not fighting any obtuse systems and it's fast to grok and edit. 

In addition to general answers to my question:

I am wondering about the second 80% of the 80/20 rule [1]. When you're iterating and polishing over and over on a semi-finished part of the game, is it a slow process? The comparison I envision is (me) knowing exactly what line of code to change versus writing up a prompt and waiting for it to process. Do thousands of small adjustments add up over time and eat away at the early gains?

It's obvious the first 80% of the work has compressed months into weeks, but the complexity is still there.

[1] The first 80% of development takes 20% of the time, and the last 20% takes 80% of the time.

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body:
I’m gonna be honest because I was reading your post and I kind of feel bad for you in a way. Obviously you must be beyond brilliant to write your own game engine, unquestionable, but then I thought about how much energy you’re spending in writing testing and maintaining the game engine when you could literally have so much functionality there for free and you can focus on making the game actually- the actual parts that the players are going to see and enjoy. I could be completely wrong and your engine could become the main takeaway from this project but ultimately there’s probably an analog feature for most of what you’ve created that has already been reviewed by the community used by game developers and maybe even working in finish products right now and that you are reinventing the mouse trap.

So I guess it depends on what you value, i’m building tools and techniques that work on top of the game engine, but I get to focus on the player experience, which is everything to me. So the answer your question the trade-offs are that I just have to trust that the technology works and I do sometimes have to explain things like I would do a little child whereas AI can be incredibly brilliant and it can be dumb as bricks.

comments.author: Jolly-Rip5973
comments.body:
Most of the people in this group aren't serious software engineers that have spent five years creating a game. 

Some of them are one prompting clones of basic games. 

Some of them have no coding experience whatsoever and 100 percent vibe coding.   
  
There are some indie devs on here but they are looking to make something in one week to six months and to not some massively complex game. 

Occasionally, I see posts from actual indie devs wanting to know how to use AI to create specific game assets. Using Ai for game assets will be the industry standard in very short order even by the AAA studios. 

The tech debt can be huge with vibe coding, because when something break, no one understands the code and it takes a long time for an actual software engineer to go through the code to fix the errors.

replies.author: RuinousFate
replies.body: As someone using AI gen assets, they still have real problems with consistency, etc.

replies.author: Jolly-Rip5973
replies.body:
You have to use LoRA files and you have to have workflows that includes quality control and manual clean-up. 

These games studios are training AI model on their own artwork or concept art either as a fine tune or LoRA files. Then they pass the assets off to real artists to clean them up and embellish them. 

The Art director is still approving or disapproving each assets if it doesn't coherently fit into the game both in terms of art style and aesthetic.

comments.author: Vumsy101
comments.body:
For me, it's been pretty crazy protyping concepts with. It's way faster to aggressively iterate and restart prototypes. And it lowers the barrier of entry on complex game genres that need a lot of moving parts to come together.

RTS, 3D fighters, tycoon games, etc.

It's also pretty good at having code underneath, while the design facing tuning can be done with quickly made plugins or cvs data tables.

I've liked its low LOD output a lot, it can make a lot of background filler stuff quickly, but high fidelity consumer facing stuff is still incoherent and generic "AI Slop".

Other than that, I'm not happy with rigging and skeleton animations. It can do some extremely basic shit, but any flair or complexity makes it shit itself.

I think for coding and such, it's better off setting up functionality and design levers for human tuning. Here's a bunch of things that do things on a scale from 0-1, then a human designer assigns 0, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 basically.

comments.author: newgenesisscion
comments.body:
I spend more time planning what to do, than implementing. 

At first it's rapid but past a certain point you really have to think about what to add/change.

comments.author: Mistah_Swick
comments.body:
I’m a developer as well, and I’ve been working on my own game for almost 1 year now, it’s a very complex game, I too am a C++ dev familiar in c++, I’ve also helped some friends with their custom engines they wrote using glfw and glm libraries. 

Anyway, to answer your question, I use ai but I have to review every line of code to make sure it is not making spaghetti, the problem with ai I have is I have 22 classes and sometimes the ai will just add a new member function or write a whole new class for something despite already having the class written. So often I stop it while it’s working and then write in more detail where in my code is needs to adjust the values/add lines etc. so you can have issues with bad structure of your code base if you let it happen because you get complacent using the tool, but honestly, it is so much faster to iterate now, especially when you are a developer who knows what they are doing. I read more code than I write it now, and for me, I don’t mind at all, because my goal isn’t to write/create the code base, the game I’m building is my goal, code is a means to an end for me it always has been. I learned c++ to get into software development, then learned js when I wanted to build a discord bot that handled my item management using Bungies API for the game Destiny 2, then learned python when I got into machine learning, and I’m back to c++, I don’t need to write an entire custom engine, I just use and change what I want from unreals source code. 

AI is progressing fast, I need to fix errors less and less, but at the end of the day, it’s what you want to do, what is fun to you. I like writing code, but that’s not why I got into programming. It was to build things. Just be prepared for the people who will say “you aren’t building it” or who will tear you down, they will be in every aspect of your life forever. Elitists are everywhere. Just ignore them lol sorry for the format or bad spelling I’m on mobile and not going back to edit it. Good luck, feel free to dm me if you have more questions! Or write here, I’m sure the info will help others too.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
> I'm making a complex game, so one of the reasons I built my own engine is because I thought over the long term, the decision would benefit me. 

Do you still think that’s true?

I don’t think that *because your game is complex* is a good reason why you would choose to make your own engine or reuse an existing one. If you’re working solo, your game is probably way, way less complex than games made by full-time teams.

> When you're iterating and polishing over and over on a semi-finished part of the game, is it a slow process?

When some part of the dev process gets slow, I figure out ways to speed it up. As you make changes, the process naturally gets slower over time. You have to make an investment and choose to spend time speeding it up again.

That can mean fixing your build system, adding tools to change things at runtime rather than compile-time, or it could mean refactoring code that is hard to change.
